Networks of regulation actions from event logs with the psychnets R package

Mohammed Saqr

University of Eastern Finland

Sonsoles López-Pernas

University of Eastern Finland
Source: vignettes/group-networks-from-event-data.Rmd
group-networks-from-event-data.Rmd

Digital learning environments produce event logs that identify the learner, the action performed and the time of the event. In collaborative tasks, these records may capture planning, monitoring, discussion, consensus building and emotional regulation. Researchers often want to know whether such actions tend to occur together, rather than merely how frequently each action occurs. Psychological network analysis offers a way to examine these patterns by representing actions as nodes and their conditional associations as edges. This approach treats relationships among observed variables as the object of analysis, while avoiding the assumption that an association represents a causal influence (Borsboom et al., 2021).

To construct a psychological network from an event log, events must first be aggregated into comparable observations. For example, counting each student’s actions produces a table with one row per student and one column per action. A Gaussian graphical model then estimates partial correlations between action frequencies, accounting for the other actions in the model (Epskamp et al., 2018). This can reveal associations that are not apparent from separate frequency summaries. However, aggregation changes the question being answered. A network comparing students’ total counts describes differences between students, whereas a network based on deviations from each student’s usual session counts describes variation within students. These levels should not be interpreted interchangeably, a distinction also relevant to the interpretation of longitudinal models (Hamaker et al., 2015).

Psychological and related network approaches have been used in education to investigate the interconnections among learning activities and regulatory processes (Saqr et al., 2024). For example, network analysis has been applied to individual monitoring events and phases of regulation in collaborative learning (Malmberg et al., 2022). Work on self-regulation has also framed learners’ behaviour as a complex, evolving system (Saqr & López-Pernas, 2024). These applications make the level of analysis especially important: group-level patterns of engagement need not reflect the processes of individual learners (Saqr, 2024). Networks based on event frequencies are therefore useful descriptive tools, but they do not by themselves establish the order of actions or the mechanisms that produce them.

This article demonstrates how to use psychnet() in psychnets to estimate networks of regulation actions from an event log. We first construct a network from each student’s complete action history and examine its edges and numerical convergence. We then compare networks estimated separately for high and low achievers. Finally, we divide the histories into sessions, estimate a network of within-student deviations and separate within-student from between-student associations. The example uses synthetic data, so the results illustrate interpretation and reporting rather than provide evidence about actual learners.

library(psychnets)

The model

For actor aa, occasion ss and action jj, the frequency is the number of matching events,

Vasj=∑eI(Ae=a,Se=s,Je=j). V_{asj} = \sum_e I(A_e = a,\ S_e = s,\ J_e = j).

Without sessions, each actor contributes one frequency vector based on the full observation period. Associations in this network therefore describe differences between actors. With sessions, each actor contributes several frequency vectors, allowing variation across occasions to be examined. Subtracting the actor’s mean, VasjW=Vasj−V‾a⋅jV^{W}_{asj} = V_{asj} - \bar V_{a \cdot j}, gives the within-actor deviations, and the actor means V‾a⋅j\bar V_{a \cdot j} carry the between-actor part. Each network is a Gaussian graphical model estimated by the EBIC graphical lasso. An edge represents a partial correlation between two action frequencies conditional on the other seven actions. Its sign indicates the direction of the association, and its magnitude indicates its estimated strength. Neither a positive nor a negative edge establishes causation.

Data

group_regulation_long, from the optional tna package, is a synthetic log of students’ regulation actions during collaborative learning, with 27,533 events from 2,000 students.

  • Actor: Actor, the student identifier.
  • Action: Action, one of nine regulation actions: adapt, cohesion, consensus, coregulate, discuss, emotion, monitor, plan and synthesis. These are the network nodes.
  • Time: Time, the timestamp of the event, used to divide each history into sessions.
  • Grouping: Achiever, high or low achievement, with 1,000 students in each.
  • Other columns: Group (collaboration group) and Course, not used here.
data("group_regulation_long", package = "tna")
event_log <- data.frame(group_regulation_long)
head(event_log)
#>   Actor Achiever Group Course                Time    Action
#> 1     1     High     1      A 2025-01-01 08:27:07  cohesion
#> 2     1     High     1      A 2025-01-01 08:35:20 consensus
#> 3     1     High     1      A 2025-01-01 08:42:18   discuss
#> 4     1     High     1      A 2025-01-01 08:50:00 synthesis
#> 5     1     High     1      A 2025-01-01 08:52:25     adapt
#> 6     1     High     1      A 2025-01-01 08:57:31 consensus

Each row records one action by one student at a particular time. Multiple rows for the same student make up that student’s event history. psychnet() recognises the data as an event log when the actor argument identifies the student column; the action column is Action by default. As the example is synthetic, its frequencies and associations should not be generalised to a population of students.

Which actions co-occur across students?

With actor = "Actor", psychnet() counts each student’s actions and estimates a graphical lasso network of the counts.

actor_net <- psychnet(data = event_log, actor = "Actor")
summary(actor_net)
#> <psychnet> glasso network
#>   nodes: 9   edges: 28   (undirected)
#>   lambda: 0.008001   gamma: 0.5
#>   optimality (KKT residual): 3.19e-11
#>   edge weight: range [-0.154, 0.434], mean 0.104
as.data.frame(actor_net)
#>          from         to       weight
#> 1       adapt   cohesion  0.028340228
#> 2    cohesion  consensus  0.104456298
#> 3       adapt coregulate  0.083642924
#> 4    cohesion coregulate  0.024349135
#> 5   consensus coregulate  0.225910826
#> 6       adapt    discuss  0.171392767
#> 7    cohesion    discuss  0.027060667
#> 8   consensus    discuss  0.329359608
#> 9  coregulate    discuss  0.115303519
#> 10      adapt    emotion -0.071536621
#> 11   cohesion    emotion  0.348144853
#> 12  consensus    emotion  0.173584152
#> 13 coregulate    emotion  0.102035538
#> 14    discuss    emotion  0.044301431
#> 15      adapt    monitor  0.027444520
#> 16 coregulate    monitor  0.063156831
#> 17    discuss    monitor  0.157029937
#> 18    emotion    monitor  0.037567027
#> 19  consensus       plan  0.434452415
#> 20 coregulate       plan -0.007036661
#> 21    discuss       plan -0.154478241
#> 22    emotion       plan  0.072573204
#> 23    monitor       plan  0.146170265
#> 24      adapt  synthesis  0.188381634
#> 25  consensus  synthesis  0.079776529
#> 26 coregulate  synthesis  0.007569019
#> 27    discuss  synthesis  0.186580959
#> 28    emotion  synthesis -0.020637713

Of the 36 possible connections between nine actions, 28 have non-zero estimated weights. These range from -0.154 to 0.434. The largest positive edge connects consensus and plan (0.434). Students with higher planning counts also tend to have higher consensus counts after accounting for their frequencies of the other seven actions. Other relatively strong positive edges connect cohesion and emotion (0.348), consensus and discuss (0.329), and consensus and coregulate (0.226).

The most negative edge connects discuss and plan (-0.154), indicating an inverse conditional association across students. This does not imply that discussion prevents planning. Some retained edges have negligible magnitudes, including coregulate–plan (-0.007) and coregulate–synthesis (0.008), and should not be given substantive interpretations simply because they are non-zero. Taken together, the comparatively strong connections involving consensus suggest that consensus building occupies a prominent position in this estimated network.

Is the fitted network the optimum of its objective?

The graphical lasso solves a penalised optimisation problem. Its solution should satisfy the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker optimality conditions. The certificate measures the remaining violation of these conditions, with a value close to zero indicating that the numerical solution meets them to high precision. This is a check on optimisation, not on whether the model is substantively correct.

certificate(actor_net)
#>   method  certificate kind certified
#> 1 glasso 3.188688e-11  kkt      TRUE

The certificate is 3.19×10−113.19 \times 10^{-11} and is marked as certified in the output. This indicates that the fitted network satisfies the graphical-lasso optimality conditions to high numerical precision at the selected penalty. It does not establish that the estimated edges would replicate in another sample.

What does the network look like?

cograph::splot() draws the network, with green positive and red negative edges and a ring showing each action’s predictability.

cograph::splot(actor_net, psych_styling = TRUE)

The figure shows consensus at the centre, with its thick edges to plan and discuss, and the cohesion–emotion pair. Node positions come from a layout algorithm and carry no statistical meaning.

Do high and low achievers differ?

With group = "Achiever", psychnet() estimates one network per achievement level and returns them together.

achievement_nets <- psychnet(data = event_log, actor = "Actor",
                             group = "Achiever")
achievement_nets
#> <psychnet_group> 2 networks by Achiever (method: glasso)
#>  group nodes edges    n
#>   High     9    25 1000
#>    Low     9    27 1000
summary(achievement_nets)
#>   group nodes edges mean_abs_weight
#> 1  High     9    25       0.1141111
#> 2   Low     9    27       0.1139959

The network for high achievers contains 25 edges and the network for low achievers contains 27, each estimated from 1,000 students. Their mean absolute weights are almost identical (0.114 in both). Thus, the average magnitude of the retained edges is very similar, although the number and arrangement of edges differ. Node strength, the sum of the absolute weights of edges connected to a node, provides a further descriptive comparison:

net_centralities(achievement_nets)
#> <psychnet_centrality_group> 2 groups: High, Low
#> 
#> --- High ---
#>         node  strength expected_influence
#> 1      adapt 0.2557087          0.2557087
#> 2   cohesion 0.4572828          0.4572828
#> 3  consensus 1.4481964          1.4481964
#> 4 coregulate 0.4826224          0.4826224
#> 5    discuss 0.9148080          0.7172144
#> 6    emotion 0.7213529          0.7213529
#> 7    monitor 0.3386263          0.3386263
#> 8       plan 0.7092177          0.5116240
#> 9  synthesis 0.3777409          0.3777409
#> 
#> --- Low ---
#>         node  strength expected_influence
#> 1      adapt 0.5044549          0.4798929
#> 2   cohesion 0.5561617          0.5561617
#> 3  consensus 1.2000886          1.2000886
#> 4 coregulate 0.6383543          0.6383543
#> 5    discuss 1.0808622          0.9531748
#> 6    emotion 0.6868285          0.6868285
#> 7    monitor 0.4027815          0.4027815
#> 8       plan 0.6447291          0.4924798
#> 9  synthesis 0.4415186          0.4415186

consensus has the highest strength in both groups, at 1.448 for high achievers and 1.200 for low achievers. For low achievers, discuss has a strength of 1.081. Both adapt (0.504 versus 0.256) and coregulate (0.638 versus 0.483) have greater strength in the low-achiever network than in the high-achiever network. The high-achiever network appears more concentrated around consensus, whereas several other actions are relatively more connected in the low-achiever network. These observations describe estimated networks and do not establish statistically significant group differences. A formal assessment requires a network comparison test (net_compare()).

cograph::splot(achievement_nets, psych_styling = TRUE)

The two panels share one layout, so each action has the same position in both.

Which actions co-occur within students?

With time = "Time", psychnet() divides each student’s history into sessions, starting a new session after a pause longer than time_threshold seconds, here five minutes. The timestamps define the sessions only; no lagged or temporal effect is estimated. With standardize = TRUE, the default, each session’s counts are centred on the student’s mean, and one network is estimated from the pooled deviations.

within_net <- psychnet(data = event_log, actor = "Actor", time = "Time",
                       time_threshold = 300)
summary(within_net)
#> <psychnet> glasso network
#>   nodes: 9   edges: 14   (undirected)
#>   lambda: 0.0288   gamma: 0.5
#>   optimality (KKT residual): 1.30e-12
#>   edge weight: range [-0.074, 0.148], mean 0.042
as.data.frame(within_net)
#>          from         to       weight
#> 1       adapt   cohesion  0.020792318
#> 2    cohesion coregulate  0.004241206
#> 3   consensus coregulate  0.057999059
#> 4       adapt    discuss  0.033506053
#> 5   consensus    discuss  0.058347732
#> 6  coregulate    discuss  0.038807994
#> 7    cohesion    emotion  0.147896226
#> 8  coregulate    monitor  0.004845725
#> 9       adapt       plan -0.015897821
#> 10   cohesion       plan -0.005337637
#> 11  consensus       plan  0.116101114
#> 12    discuss       plan -0.073852486
#> 13      adapt  synthesis  0.089102215
#> 14    discuss  synthesis  0.116874946
certificate(within_net)
#>   method  certificate kind certified
#> 1 glasso 1.296872e-12  kkt      TRUE

The within-student network contains 14 edges, compared with 28 in the network based on students’ complete histories. The selected penalty is λ=0.0288\lambda = 0.0288, compared with 0.0080 for the full-history network. The largest within-student edge connects cohesion and emotion (0.148). In sessions where a student has more cohesion events than their own average, they also tend to have more emotion events than their own average, conditional on the other actions. Further positive edges connect discuss–synthesis (0.117) and consensus–plan (0.116), while discuss–plan is negative (-0.074).

The certificate is 1.30×10−121.30 \times 10^{-12}, indicating a numerically satisfactory graphical-lasso solution. The smaller number of edges and lower maximum weight describe a sparser, generally weaker set of conditional associations than in the full-history network. These differences must be interpreted cautiously because the networks use different observational units and have different selected penalties. In particular, an association between students need not also characterise how a given student varies across sessions.

cograph::splot(within_net, psych_styling = TRUE)

How do the within- and between-student networks compare?

With standardize = FALSE, psychnet() keeps both parts of the session data: the within-student network of the deviations and the between-student network of the students’ mean session counts.

multilevel_nets <- psychnet(data = event_log, actor = "Actor", time = "Time",
                            time_threshold = 300, standardize = FALSE)
multilevel_nets
#> <psychnet_multilevel> glasso networks (within + between)
#>   actors: 2000   occasions: 12305
#>   within : 9 nodes, 14 edges
#>   between: 9 nodes, 24 edges

Applying the five-minute session rule to the histories of 2,000 students produces 12,305 sessions. The decomposition yields 14 edges in the within-student network and 24 in the between-student network of average session counts. These are two distinct sources of association: deviations within students and differences between students’ average session profiles. The between-student component has more retained edges in this fitted model, but edge counts alone do not demonstrate stronger underlying processes. The plot presents the two networks side by side.

cograph::splot(multilevel_nets, psych_styling = TRUE)

This decomposition separates within-student from between-student covariance in the session-level counts. It is not a random-effects model, and neither component describes the temporal ordering of regulatory actions. Also, the between-student network here is based on mean session counts, so it is not the same estimand as the earlier network based on complete-history counts.

Reporting the analysis

To make an event-log network analysis reproducible, a report should specify the actor and action columns and, when applicable, the time column. It should explain how events were counted, what constitutes an observation, and how sessions were defined. The report should distinguish whole-history, within-student and between-student estimands, identify the estimator and its settings, and present the main edge patterns with appropriate caution. Dividing a log by timestamps does not make a contemporaneous association network a temporal or causal model.

For example, the synthetic log contains 27,533 events from 2,000 students. The network of complete-history counts contains 28 edges, with consensus having several of the strongest connections. The networks of high and low achievers contain 25 and 27 edges, respectively, and both have a mean absolute edge weight of approximately 0.114. A five-minute session rule identifies 12,305 sessions. The session-based analysis produces a within-student network with 14 edges and a between-student network of average session counts with 24 edges. These figures describe the fitted example, not population-level effects.

Assumptions and when to use which network

  • The between-actor network (actor only) answers how students who differ in one action differ in others. It needs one observation per student and many students.
  • The within-actor network (time or session, standardize = TRUE) answers how an actor’s actions vary together from session to session. It needs several sessions per actor, and the session rule should be fixed in advance and checked for sensitivity.
  • standardize = FALSE keeps both, which shows whether an association is a difference between actors, a variation within them, or both.
  • Counts are skewed and the graphical lasso assumes approximate normality; the nonparanormal model (method = "huge") is a sensitivity check.
  • Edges are associations between action frequencies, not between individual events, and not causal effects. For the order in which actions follow one another, transition network analysis is the appropriate model.
